result.topic_en: Euler expresses the coefficients of Lagrange's canonical integral equation in terms of the quartic's coefficients A–E and the constant Γ, notes that the rationalized integral covers both dx/√X ± dy/√Y = 0, and recalls an alternative form of the integral.

§. 44. Hinc ergo pro aequatione canonica literae graecae $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$, etc. per latinas A, B, C, D, E, vna cum conſtante $\Gamma$ ſequenti modo determinantur:
$\alpha = 4AC + 4\Gamma A - BB$
$\beta = 2AD + \Gamma B$
$\gamma = 4AE - \Gamma\Gamma$
$\delta = BD + 4AE + \Gamma^2 + 2\Gamma C$
$\varepsilon = 2BE + \Gamma D$
$\zeta = 4CE + 4\Gamma E - DD$
ita vt aequatio canonica, qua olim ſum vſus, ſit
$\alpha + 2\beta(x+y) + \gamma(xx+yy) + 2\delta xy$
$+ 2\varepsilon xy(x+y) + \zeta xxyy = 0.$

§. 45. Haec autem aequatio integralis ad rationalitatem perducta latius patet quam aequatio propoſita differentialis $\frac{dx}{\surd X} - \frac{dy}{\surd Y} = 0$: ſimul enim complectitur integrale huius: $\frac{dx}{\surd X} + \frac{dy}{\surd Y} = 0$. Scilicet haec aequatio complectitur duos factores, quorum alteruter alterutri ſatisfacit. Ex geneſi autem patet hanc aequationem eſſe productum ex his factoribus: $\Delta(x-y)^2 - V + 2\surd XY$, et $\Delta(x-y)^2 - V - 2\surd XY$.

§. 46. Supra iam obſeruauimus, eiusdem aequationis differentialis integrale hoc quoque modo exhiberi poſſe:
$\frac{M\surd Y + N\surd X}{(x-y)^3} = C$ (vide §. 8. et praec.) exiſtente
$M = 4A + B(3x+y) + 2C(xx+xy)$
$+ Dxx(x+3y) + 4Ex^3y$
$N = 4A + B(3y+x) + 2Cy(x+y)$
$+ Dyy(y+3x) + 4Exy^3$

items.quote: Haec autem aequatio integralis ad rationalitatem perducta latius patet quam aequatio propoſita differentialis $\frac{dx}{\surd X} - \frac{dy}{\surd Y} = 0$: ſimul enim complectitur integrale huius: $\frac{dx}{\surd X} + \frac{dy}{\surd Y} = 0$.
items.english: This integral equation, once made rational, extends further than the proposed differential equation dx/√X − dy/√Y = 0: it simultaneously contains the integral of dx/√X + dy/√Y = 0.

items.quote: Ex geneſi autem patet hanc aequationem eſſe productum ex his factoribus: $\Delta(x-y)^2 - V + 2\surd XY$, et $\Delta(x-y)^2 - V - 2\surd XY$.
items.english: From its derivation it is clear that this equation is the product of the factors Δ(x−y)² − V + 2√XY and Δ(x−y)² − V − 2√XY.

items.quote: Supra iam obſeruauimus, eiusdem aequationis differentialis integrale hoc quoque modo exhiberi poſſe:
items.english: We already observed above that the integral of the same differential equation can also be expressed in this way: (M√Y + N√X)/(x−y)³ = C.
